The word pawn has three distinct meanings. All three are common, so knowing all of them is important.

In the game of chess, a pawn is the smallest and most common piece on the board. Each player starts with eight pawns — more than any other piece. They stand in a row at the front, like foot soldiers guarding the more powerful pieces behind them.

Pawns are generally considered the weakest pieces on the board because they can only move forward, one step at a time, and they capture enemies only by moving diagonally. They have very limited freedom compared to pieces like the queen, bishop, or knight.

However, pawns have one remarkable ability: if a pawn manages to travel all the way to the other end of the board, it gets promoted — it transforms into any powerful piece you choose, almost always a queen. This makes pawns more valuable than they first appear.

Example sentence:
"He lost three pawns in the first few moves and was already in a weak position."
Meaning 2: A Person Who Is Used and Manipulated

This is the figurative (non-literal) meaning of pawn, and it is used very frequently in everyday language.

When you call someone a pawn, you mean they are a person who is being used or controlled by someone more powerful, often to serve that powerful person's own goals — and usually without having much say in the matter. A pawn, in this sense, doesn't make the big decisions; they are simply moved around and used as a tool, just like a chess pawn is moved around the board by the player.

This meaning carries a slightly sad or critical tone — it implies the person is not truly in control of their own situation and may even be unaware of how they are being used.

Example sentences:

  • "The poor villagers were mere pawns in the politicians' power struggle."
  • "She realized too late that she had been a pawn in his scheme to take over the company."

A key thing to understand: being called a pawn does not mean the person is stupid or bad. It simply means someone more powerful is pulling the strings, and this person is the one being moved around.
Meaning 3: Something Given as Security for a Loan

This meaning comes from the world of money-lending and is directly connected to the idea of a pawnshop (also called a pawnbroker's shop).

Here is how it works: Imagine you need money urgently but you don't have cash. You can take a valuable item you own — say, a gold ring, a watch, or a musical instrument — to a pawnbroker (a special kind of moneylender). You hand over that item temporarily, and in return, the pawnbroker gives you a cash loan.

That item you hand over is called a pawn.

Now, you have an agreed period of time to repay the loan plus interest. If you do, you get your item back. If you fail to repay, the pawnbroker keeps your item and sells it to recover their money.

So a pawn, in this sense, is essentially an object held as a guarantee — it assures the lender that they won't lose their money, because they can always sell the object if you don't pay up.

Example sentences:

  • "He left his grandfather's watch as a pawn to borrow enough money for the rent."
  • "She redeemed her pawn — the silver bracelet — once she got her salary."

The common phrases you'll encounter:

  • "In pawn" means an item is currently being held by the pawnbroker. ("My camera is in pawn right now.")
  • "Redeem a pawn" means paying back the loan to get your item back.

If you step back and look at all three meanings, you'll notice they all share a common thread: something of value that is placed under someone else's control, with limited power of its own.

  • A chess pawn is the most controlled, least free piece on the board.
  • A person who is a pawn is controlled by someone more powerful.
  • An object given as a pawn is held under someone else's control until a debt is settled.

Understanding this common thread will help you remember and feel all three meanings deeply, not just memorize them.
